subject: history_social
passage: Night markets in Bangkok, Thailand, attract both residents and tourists. Urban geographer Niran Chaiyaporn counted the stalls of each type at two night markets, one near a business district popular with visitors and one in a residential neighborhood. He hypothesized that the residential market would devote a much larger share of its stalls to everyday goods, such as fresh produce and household items, than the business district market would.

data.title: Stalls at Two Bangkok Night Markets

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chaiyaporn's hypothesis?

choices.A: About 48% of stalls at the residential market sold produce or household goods, versus 13% at the other market.
choices.B: The business district market had more prepared-food stalls than the residential market had, 120 compared with 95.
choices.C: The residential market had more clothing and souvenir stalls than the business district market, 140 compared with 30.
choices.D: Most shoppers at the residential market said they lived within a short walk of it and visited weekly.

explanation.why: The hypothesis is about the share of each market's stalls selling everyday goods. The residential market has 60 + 55 = 115 such stalls out of 240 (about 48%), while the business district market has 15 + 25 = 40 out of 300 (about 13%).
explanation.A: Correct. Everyday goods filled about 48% of the residential market's stalls but only about 13% of the business district market's, as the hypothesis predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but prepared food is not one of the everyday goods named in the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This swaps the markets: the business district market had 140 clothing and souvenir stalls, and the residential market had 30.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table counts stalls; it contains no information about shoppers.
